paragraphs: Adversarial examples usually highlight how a small input change can cause a neural network to change its answer. This paper investigates a different problem: large, deliberately chosen changes can sometimes leave the network's internal representation essentially unchanged. The network can therefore overlook substantial differences between inputs, even while being sensitive to other, much smaller changes.

The authors connect this behavior to intrinsic properties of the ReLU activation function. They call it a feature collision when different examples produce the same feature activation and consequently receive the same classification decision. This shifts attention from the final prediction to the intermediate representation: two inputs can become indistinguishable to the classifier because their differences disappear in its features.

The empirical findings suggest these collisions are abundant. The authors demonstrate geometric regions called polytopes containing approximately colliding examples near practically any example examined. The result concerns approximate agreement across regions, rather than only isolated matching pairs. It identifies excessive insensitivity as another way neural representations can fail to preserve meaningful input differences.
neurips-2019-approximate-feature-collisi.tldr: Neural networks can map substantially different inputs to nearly identical features, with experiments finding abundant regions of such collisions.

paragraphs: A classifier trained on biased data can carry those biases into its decisions, potentially producing inequitable treatment. Finding these problems often requires people to label existing examples and inspect where the classifier fails. That approach is constrained by the labor involved and by which images happen to be available for examination.

This paper proposes interrogating classifiers with generated facial images. A progressive conditional generative model synthesizes photorealistic faces, providing a source of examples for probing an independent classification system. Bayesian optimization guides the interrogation efficiently. Together, image generation and guided search turn bias characterization into a systematic simulation process rather than an examination limited to a fixed image collection.

The authors demonstrate that this approach can efficiently characterize racial and gender biases in commercial systems. The contribution is a method for investigating classifier behavior using synthesized inputs, with search helping direct the investigation. Its stated outcome is the characterization of bias; the abstract does not claim that generating these examples automatically corrects the classifiers being examined.
neurips-2019-characterizing-bias-in-clas.tldr: Generated facial images and Bayesian optimization provide a systematic way to characterize racial and gender biases in commercial classifiers.

paragraphs: Navigation instructions describe more than a destination: they imply observations and actions that should occur along a successful route. This paper uses that idea to formulate vision-and-language navigation as Bayesian state tracking. The agent reasons about possible states and trajectories, maintaining a probability distribution that expresses uncertainty about how the instructions fit its surroundings.

A mapper builds a semantic spatial map as navigation proceeds. Learned observation and motion models are conditioned on the events expected from the instructions. These components form an end-to-end differentiable Bayes filter, trained to locate the goal by predicting the most likely instructed trajectory through the map. The explicit spatial and probabilistic structure also makes the approach more explainable.

Experiments show better goal-location prediction on the map than a strong LingUNet baseline. For the complete task of actually navigating to the destination, the authors report promising results with less dependence on navigation constraints. These are distinct findings: stronger map-based goal prediction supports the approach, while the full navigation result is described more cautiously.
neurips-2019-chasing-ghosts-instruction-.tldr: A learned Bayesian filter follows navigation instructions by tracking probable trajectories through a semantic map built during exploration.

paragraphs: Distributed neural network training can spend substantial time communicating gradients between workers. Compressing these messages reduces traffic, but compression must still support reliable optimization. The paper notes that signSGD with majority vote offers a 32-fold communication reduction, yet its convergence analysis uses unrealistic assumptions and the method can diverge in practice.

The proposed framework combines compressed stochastic gradient descent with Nesterov momentum and considers compression in both communication directions. Its analysis establishes convergence results for nonconvex problems using general gradient compressors. A specific blockwise compressor partitions the gradient, representing each block with one-bit values and a scaling factor. This achieves nearly a 32-fold reduction in communication.

In the reported experiments, the method matches the convergence speed and testing accuracy of full-precision distributed momentum SGD. For ResNet training on ImageNet with seven workers, it reaches the same testing accuracy with 46% less wall-clock time. This separates the reduction in transmitted information from the measured training speedup: the latter reflects the complete distributed training process.
neurips-2019-communication-efficient-dis.tldr: Two-way blockwise gradient compression supports distributed momentum training with nearly 32-fold less communication and substantial measured training-time savings.

paragraphs: Archetypal analysis describes each data instance as a mixture of representative prototypes called archetypes. These prototypes sit on the boundary of the data's convex hull, giving them a geometric connection to the observed examples. This often makes them easier to interpret than factors from other matrix factorization methods, but enforcing the required convexity constraints adds computational cost.

The paper addresses that cost by constructing coresets: compact representations that allow the analysis to work with less data while retaining a provable approximation guarantee. Its central theoretical connection uses the quantization error of k-means to upper-bound the archetypal analysis error. This provides a way to control what is lost when the original data are summarized.

The authors show that a provable absolute-coreset can be computed in two passes over the data. They also report improved empirical performance on several datasets. The contribution therefore links an interpretable representation method to an efficient summarization strategy, supporting its use without requiring every stage of the analysis to operate on the complete dataset.
neurips-2019-coresets-for-archetypal-ana.tldr: Two-pass coresets make archetypal analysis more efficient while providing approximation guarantees derived from k-means quantization error.

paragraphs: Fair clustering adds representation constraints to objectives such as k-means and k-median. In the setting described here, clusters should approximately reflect the underlying proportions of sensitive groups. Handling multiple overlapping attributes complicates this requirement because one person or point can belong to several groups simultaneously. The paper addresses scalability while retaining this richer group structure.

The method constructs coresets that summarize the dataset for fairness-constrained clustering. For k-median, the stated size is O(Γk²ε⁻ᵈ); for k-means, it is O(Γk³ε⁻ᵈ⁻¹). Here Γ counts distinct combinations of group memberships. These bounds avoid dependence on the full dataset size, although they still depend on dimension, approximation precision, cluster count, and membership combinations.

The authors provide the first known fair k-median coreset construction and extend fair k-means coresets to overlapping attributes. Combining the summaries with existing algorithms yields the fastest algorithms for several cases. Experiments on Adult and Bank find substantially smaller summaries and faster fair-clustering objective computation, with a small difference in the resulting objective.
neurips-2019-coresets-for-clustering-wit.tldr: Compact coresets accelerate clustering with fairness constraints across multiple overlapping groups while controlling changes to the clustering objective.

paragraphs: Binary activation functions give neural network units a discrete output, creating a challenge for training because the activation function is not differentiable. This paper studies multilayer networks with these activations through PAC-Bayesian theory. It brings together two questions: how to train the networks end to end and how to give meaningful guarantees about their generalization.

The approach minimizes the expected loss of an aggregation of binary-activated networks, with the aggregation depending on the architecture. This formulation is central to both the training framework and its analysis. The authors state that their analysis inherently overcomes the nondifferentiability of binary activation, making discrete activation compatible with the proposed learning procedure.

The theoretical contribution includes nonvacuous PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds, meaning bounds that provide informative guarantees rather than an unhelpful ceiling on error. The method is also assessed through a thorough numerical protocol on real-world datasets. Together, these contributions connect practical training with a formal account of generalization for the same family of binary-activated deep networks.
neurips-2019-dichotomize-and-generalize-.tldr: An aggregation-based framework trains binary-activated deep networks and provides informative PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds.

paragraphs: Posterior collapse occurs when some latent variables in a variational autoencoder have posterior distributions close to their uninformative priors. Those variables then convey little information about the particular input. This paper investigates the phenomenon in linear VAEs, using their direct connection to probabilistic principal component analysis to make the underlying optimization behavior easier to understand.

The analysis shows that collapse can arise from local maxima in the marginal likelihood of probabilistic PCA itself. For a linear VAE, the authors prove that optimizing the evidence lower bound, or ELBO, introduces no additional spurious local maxima relative to that likelihood. They also show that training with exact variational inference recovers a uniquely identifiable global maximum associated with principal component directions.

These results locate a possible source of collapse in the likelihood landscape rather than assigning it automatically to the variational objective. Experiments indicate that the linear analysis is predictive even for high-capacity nonlinear VAEs. In particular, it helps explain how observation noise, local maxima, and collapse are related in deep Gaussian VAEs.
neurips-2019-don-t-blame-the-elbo-a-line.tldr: Linear VAE analysis shows that posterior collapse can originate in likelihood local maxima without the ELBO introducing additional spurious maxima.

paragraphs: This paper studies overconstrained linear regression when prediction errors are measured with a symmetric norm. Such a norm treats an error vector the same after coordinates are reordered or their signs are flipped. The aim is to solve regression efficiently across this broad family of losses, using linear sketching and running time tied to input sparsity.

For Orlicz norms, an important subclass defined through a function applied to scaled coordinate magnitudes, the algorithm achieves a multiplicative approximation of 1 + ε for any arbitrarily small positive constant ε. This improves substantially on the previously known factor of d times a polylogarithmic function of n, where d is the number of regression parameters.

For general symmetric norms, the approximation factor is √d times polylog n times a norm-dependent quantity, mmc(ℓ). The authors describe this as the first input-sparsity-time algorithm with provable guarantees for that general setting. The results advance a common sketching approach to regression, while the possible broader usefulness of the techniques remains a proposed direction.
neurips-2019-efficient-symmetric-norm-re.tldr: Linear sketching yields input-sparsity-time regression algorithms with near-exact guarantees for Orlicz norms and broader guarantees for symmetric norms.

paragraphs: Saliency-based interpretation methods aim to show which parts of an input matter to a neural network's prediction. This paper asks whether those explanations can be deliberately changed by modifying the model while preserving its accuracy. The intervention is a fine-tuning step aimed at the explanation itself, so the object being manipulated is the trained network.

The authors place interpretation results directly into a penalty term in the fine-tuning objective. They demonstrate attacks on methods including LRP, Grad-CAM, and SimpleGrad, using models such as VGG19, ResNet50, and DenseNet121. Two forms of manipulation, called Passive and Active, produce altered explanations that generalize across the validation set and transfer to other interpretation methods.

The evaluation combines visual examples with quantitative measurements of how far explanations move from their originals. These results show that maintained predictive accuracy can coexist with substantially altered saliency explanations. The authors therefore argue that resistance to adversarial model manipulation should be a criterion when developing reliable interpretation methods, alongside the usefulness of their displayed explanations.
neurips-2019-fooling-neural-network-inte.tldr: Targeted model fine-tuning can substantially alter saliency explanations while preserving accuracy, exposing a stability problem for interpretation methods.

paragraphs: This paper introduces full-gradients as a representation for interpreting neural network responses. It separates the response into components associated with sensitivity to the input and sensitivity at individual neurons. The aim is to capture explanatory information beyond what can be expressed by a single input-focused saliency map.

The authors prove that the full-gradient representation satisfies two properties, completeness and weak dependence, that no saliency-map-based method can satisfy together. For convolutional networks, they then aggregate the full-gradient components into an approximate saliency representation called FullGrad. The distinction matters: the theoretical properties belong to the fuller representation, while the visual map is an approximation constructed from it.

The paper evaluates FullGrad using pixel perturbation and remove-and-retrain tests. The reported experiments indicate that it explains model behavior correctly and more comprehensively than comparison methods. Visual inspection also finds sharper maps concentrated more closely on object regions. The work thus pairs a theoretical argument for a richer representation with empirical evidence that its approximate visualization is useful.
neurips-2019-full-gradient-representatio.tldr: Full-gradients provide a richer theoretical representation of network responses, and their FullGrad visualization performs well in quantitative and visual evaluations.

paragraphs: Hierarchical reinforcement learning separates decisions across levels, allowing a high-level policy to work with lower-level skills. This can help with tasks whose rewards arrive only after long sequences of actions. A difficulty is making those skills adapt to the task without requiring a person to design specialized rewards for each one.

The proposed framework derives auxiliary rewards for skill learning from the advantage function of the high-level policy. That function assesses how favorable a choice is relative to the policy's reference expectation. Using it as the training signal links skill improvement to the broader task and allows high-level decisions and low-level skills to be learned simultaneously without task-specific reward knowledge.

The authors theoretically show that optimizing skills with this auxiliary reward increases the joint policy's task return. In MuJoCo experiments, they report substantially better performance than other state-of-the-art hierarchical methods. They also find that policies at both levels transfer. The contribution is a shared training principle that connects skill adaptation to the objective of the hierarchy as a whole.
neurips-2019-hierarchical-reinforcement-.tldr: High-level advantage functions supply auxiliary rewards that jointly train adaptable low-level skills and high-level policies.

paragraphs: Functional MRI measures brain activity through a hemodynamic response that unfolds much more slowly than neural spikes. This raises a question: do those slow measurements contain information relevant to cognition? The paper investigates that question by applying Gaussian Process Factor Analysis, or GPFA, and machine learning to extract smooth, low-dimensional dynamics from fMRI recordings.

The authors analyze data sampled at 1.4 Hz from 1,000 healthy Human Connectome Project participants. GPFA components with characteristic timescales below 1 Hz identify the task being performed with accuracy above 95%. Connections between these slow latent components also predict differences between individuals' behavioral scores across several cognitive tasks.

In patient analyses, dynamics below 0.1 Hz predict Clinical Dementia Rating scores and identify people with mild cognitive impairment who later develop Alzheimer's dementia. These findings show predictive information in slow brain dynamics despite the mismatch with the speed of neural spiking. The authors conclude that such dynamics may help explain cognitive function and decline, preserving a distinction between predictive associations and an established neural mechanism.
neurips-2019-infra-slow-brain-dynamics-a.tldr: Slow latent dynamics extracted from fMRI predict tasks, cognitive differences, and indicators of cognitive decline.

paragraphs: This paper approaches time-dependent data through recurrent kernel machines and derives connections to familiar neural sequence models. Within that perspective, hidden units and gated memory cells arise naturally. The contribution is a common mathematical viewpoint for understanding several architectures, together with new variants motivated by that viewpoint.

Allowing the memory gate to change dynamically produces a model closely related to an LSTM recurrent network. Extending the construction to n-gram filters recovers convolutional networks, gated convolutional networks, and recurrent additive networks as special cases. The same framework therefore connects recurrent memory with filters that operate over short sequences, and extends the LSTM-related construction to those filters.

The authors test their derived variants on natural language processing tasks and on neuroscience data involving local field potentials. They report performance matching or exceeding traditional neural methods, with significant improvements over the prior state of the art in the neuroscience application. These experiments support the practical value of the kernel perspective alongside its role in explaining relationships between model families.
neurips-2019-kernel-based-approaches-for.tldr: Recurrent kernel machines unify several neural sequence architectures and motivate variants with competitive language and neuroscience results.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation needs both broad context and fine spatial detail to assign labels across an image. The paper argues that expanding context through stacked local convolutions or non-local blocks can overlook object details because these operations do not preserve spatial structure. Its goal is to connect distant features while retaining the structure useful for detailed segmentation.

The proposed learnable tree filter uses the structural properties of a minimal spanning tree to model long-range dependencies. A linear-time algorithm makes the filtering operation efficient, and the resulting module can be inserted into existing deep networks. The authors embed these modules in a unified semantic segmentation framework.

Ablation studies examine both effectiveness and efficiency. With the same backbone network, the tree-filter approach achieves better performance with much less overhead than the classic PSP block and non-local operation. The authors also report consistent gains across several benchmarks without additional embellishments. These results support the module as a practical way to improve contextual feature processing while preserving image structure.
neurips-2019-learnable-tree-filter-for-s.tldr: A linear-time learnable tree filter captures long-range image context while preserving detail and improving semantic segmentation.

paragraphs: Robust regression becomes especially difficult when an adversary controls most examples. This paper studies a setting where only an α fraction of equations follow the intended linear relationship with small noise, while the rest are arbitrary. It seeks a short list of candidate regressors containing a good answer, rather than requiring one uniquely determined output.

The authors give the first polynomial-time algorithm for this list-decodable setting, producing O(1/α) candidates. Success requires the genuine examples to come from a certifiably anti-concentrated distribution. For standard Gaussian inliers, the running time is (d/α) raised to O(1/α⁸), making its dependence on the genuine-data fraction explicit.

For certain discrete product distributions, a similar guarantee requires the true coefficient vector to have coordinates of equal magnitude. The authors also prove that anti-concentration is information-theoretically necessary, so this condition addresses recoverability itself. Their algorithmic framework strengthens the connection between identifiability and computation using the sum-of-squares method, explaining how a recoverable candidate can be found despite majority corruption.
neurips-2019-list-decodable-linear-regre.tldr: Under anti-concentration conditions, list-decodable regression efficiently returns a short candidate list containing an accurate regressor despite majority corruption.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo tree search plans by simulating possible sequences of decisions and propagating information through a search tree. This paper modifies that process using maximum-entropy policy optimization. Its algorithm, Maximum Entropy for Tree Search, or MENTS, evaluates nodes using softmax values passed backward from simulations.

The analysis first studies stochastic softmax bandits, a single-step decision problem that isolates the value-estimation component. The authors show that softmax values can be estimated at an optimal convergence rate measured by mean squared error. They then extend this approach to sequential decisions, where the search must account for consequences across multiple steps.

For MENTS, the probability of failing to identify the best root decision decreases exponentially, improving on the polynomial convergence rate of UCT in the stated analysis. Experiments on synthetic problems and Atari 2600 games also find greater sample efficiency than UCT. The contribution therefore connects a theoretical improvement in root-decision reliability with empirical evidence that simulations can be used more efficiently.
neurips-2019-maximum-entropy-monte-carlo.tldr: Maximum-entropy tree search improves theoretical root-decision convergence and uses simulations more efficiently than UCT in reported experiments.

paragraphs: A dynamic treatment regime specifies a treatment decision at each intervention stage, using the patient's evolving treatment and covariate history. The paper studies how to learn such decision rules through online reinforcement learning. It also considers how observational records can help, even when confounding makes those records imperfect evidence about treatment dynamics.

The first contribution is an adaptive online algorithm with near-optimal regret that does not require historical data. Regret measures the loss incurred while learning relative to optimal decision-making. This establishes a learning procedure for the online setting before introducing the separate question of how existing observations should influence it.

The authors then derive informative bounds on the underlying treatment-regime dynamics from confounded observational data. They combine those bounds with the online learning results to obtain an algorithm that efficiently learns an optimal regime while using the available observations. The key connection is that imperfect historical information can still constrain learning usefully; the contribution concerns algorithmic learning guarantees rather than a reported clinical treatment trial.
neurips-2019-near-optimal-reinforcement-.tldr: Near-optimal online learning for sequential treatment decisions is combined with informative bounds derived from confounded observational data.

paragraphs: This paper asks when adversarially robust classification is learnable, considering both the number of examples required and the computation involved. Its definition requires polynomial sample complexity. The setting uses binary inputs, making the adversary's power explicit through the number of input bits it may change.

The authors prove that no nontrivial concept class is robustly learnable in the distribution-free setting even against a one-bit perturbation. For monotone conjunctions under the uniform distribution, robustness is also impossible when the perturbation budget grows faster than log n. However, when the adversary is limited to O(log n) changed bits, these concepts are robustly learnable over a general family of distributions that includes the uniform distribution.

The paper additionally proves computational hardness on the Boolean hypercube, assuming only that a hard learning problem exists in the PAC framework. Together, the results show how distributional assumptions and perturbation budgets change feasibility. The positive result is essential context: the impossibility statements apply to their specified settings, rather than to every form of robust learning.
neurips-2019-on-the-hardness-of-robust-c.tldr: Robust learning faces strong sample and computational barriers, with feasibility depending on distributional assumptions and the adversary's perturbation budget.

paragraphs: Low-rank approximation seeks a simpler representation of a matrix while controlling reconstruction error. This paper analyzes methods based on selecting original matrix columns when error is measured using an ℓp objective. The results apply to both real and complex matrices and sharpen how approximation quality depends on the desired rank k.

For column subset selection, the approximation ratio is (k + 1)^(1/p) when 1 ≤ p ≤ 2, and (k + 1)^(1 − 1/p) when p ≥ 2. These improve the previous O(k + 1) bound. Matching lower bounds establish tightness, including the constant, for p ≥ 2. The analysis draws on the Riesz–Thorin interpolation theorem from harmonic analysis.

The authors also analyze a polynomial-time method that selects O(k log m) columns, allowing extra columns in exchange for computational efficiency. It achieves the same rank dependence up to big-O factors. This bicriteria result further yields a polynomial-time exact-rank method with a slightly larger approximation ratio, connecting the sharper analysis to multiple computational tradeoffs.
neurips-2019-optimal-analysis-of-subset-.tldr: Sharper, partly tight approximation bounds improve the theory of column-selection methods for ℓp low-rank matrix approximation.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor methods use the relationships between nearby observations to identify unusual examples. This paper examines how well these familiar procedures work for anomaly detection, combining experiments with statistical analysis. Extensive simulations show favorable comparisons with some state-of-the-art alternatives on synthetic benchmarks, while real-data experiments examine how performance relates to problem dimensionality.

For the theoretical analysis, the authors study distance-to-measure, or DTM, a more general quantity originating in robust geometric and topological inference. This gives them a framework for studying the behavior behind nearest-neighbor anomaly scores. They establish finite-sample uniform guarantees for empirical DTM, controlling its accuracy across the domain rather than only at one selected point.

Those guarantees lead to misclassification rates for anomalous observations under several settings. The analysis uses Huber's contamination model and mild geometric regularity assumptions on the data distribution. These assumptions define the scope of the guarantees. The resulting contribution gives statistical support to nearest-neighbor anomaly detection alongside empirical evidence about its competitiveness and relationship to dimension.
neurips-2019-statistical-analysis-of-nea.tldr: Nearest-neighbor anomaly detection receives empirical support and finite-sample error guarantees through distance-to-measure analysis.

paragraphs: A generative model may produce samples without providing an explicit probability density that can be evaluated directly. This paper develops implicit Metropolis–Hastings for such models when the target distribution is represented by examples. It generalizes earlier ideas that use a GAN discriminator to screen out unrealistic generator outputs.

The method learns a discriminator to estimate a density ratio and uses that estimate to generate a chain of samples. Because the ratio is approximate, each step can introduce error. The important question is therefore what distribution the chain approaches over time, rather than whether individual generated samples appear plausible.

The authors provide a theoretical result linking discriminator loss to the total variation distance between the target and the chain's stationary distribution. The loss supplies an upper bound on this discrepancy, connecting discriminator quality to the eventual sampling distribution. They validate the algorithm with both independent and Markov proposals on CIFAR-10, CelebA, and ImageNet, demonstrating its application beyond a single proposal mechanism.
neurips-2019-the-implicit-metropolis-has.tldr: Implicit Metropolis–Hastings uses learned density ratios for sampling and bounds stationary-distribution error through discriminator loss.

paragraphs: Estimating a property of a distribution over a large domain can require careful use of both samples and computation. This paper develops a shared construction for sufficiently smooth additive properties, covering symmetric and nonsymmetric cases. Additive structure allows the target property to be treated through contributions associated with the distribution's individual probabilities.

The central technique is piecewise-polynomial approximation. It yields estimators computable in near-linear time, with asymptotically optimal approximation values and strong concentration. For all k-symbol Lipschitz properties, the authors obtain the stated minimax sample complexity O(k/(ε² log k)) for ε-error estimation, combining statistical efficiency with efficient computation.

The same methodology also produces near-optimal differentially private estimators for a variety of properties. Further results include optimal bias and near-optimal variance for five important properties, and near-optimal sample complexity for several symmetric properties across domain sizes and confidence levels. The contribution is the breadth of one approximation-based framework, while the precise optimality claims differ across these results.
neurips-2019-unified-sample-optimal-prop.tldr: Piecewise-polynomial approximation unifies efficient distribution-property estimators with optimal or near-optimal guarantees across several settings.

paragraphs: Predicting a video from one image requires a model to determine both how an object moves and how future frames should look. This paper conditions prediction on the starting image and an action class. It organizes generation around a sequence of keypoints, providing an intermediate representation of the object's future motion.

The model first detects keypoints on the moving object and predicts how those points evolve. It then translates the input image according to the predicted keypoint sequence to construct future frames. Keypoint detection is learned without human keypoint annotations, and detections from the original training videos serve as pseudo-labels for learning object motion.

Experiments show successful application across multiple datasets without paying the cost of labeling video keypoints. The learned points resemble human annotations, and the generated predictions are reported to look more realistic than those from previous methods. The result supports using automatically learned spatial landmarks to connect motion prediction and image generation, with an explicit action class guiding the future behavior.
neurips-2019-unsupervised-keypoint-learn.tldr: Automatically learned keypoints guide action-conditioned video prediction from a single image without requiring human keypoint labels.

paragraphs: Adversarial training improves robustness by training on deliberately perturbed inputs, but constructing those inputs can cost more than the network training itself. This paper targets that computational burden. It recasts adversarial training as a discrete-time differential game, providing a way to examine the interaction between the adversary's updates and the network's parameters.

Using Pontryagin's Maximum Principle, the authors observe that the adversary update is coupled only with the parameters of the first layer. This motivates performing most forward and backward computations for adversary updates within that layer. The resulting algorithm, YOPO, requires only one full forward and backward propagation for each group of adversary updates.

The computational saving comes from reducing repeated passes through the entire network during adversarial example generation. In numerical experiments, YOPO achieves comparable defense accuracy to projected gradient descent adversarial training while using approximately one-fifth to one-quarter of its GPU time. The result supports the proposed optimization shortcut empirically, with comparable robustness reported for the evaluated settings.
neurips-2019-you-only-propagate-once-acc.tldr: YOPO reduces full-network computation during adversarial training, achieving comparable defense accuracy with roughly one-fifth to one-quarter of PGD's GPU time.
